analysis.one_liner: Extends the 36% military interest-rate cap and loan protections to all consumers.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the House and referred to the Financial Services Committee; it has one cosponsor and no vote has been scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would extend to all Americans the credit protections that current law provides only to service members and their families. Those protections cap interest rates and fees on most consumer loans at 36% a year, limit fees and fine print like mandatory arbitration, and stop lenders from requiring access to bank accounts or paychecks as a loan condition. The bill sits in the House Financial Services Committee with a single cosponsor and no scheduled action.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary borrowers who use small-dollar and high-cost credit: people taking payday loans, installment loans, car-title loans, or overdraft-like products who could see interest and fees capped at 36% a year instead of triple-digit rates that can reach several hundred percent annually.

how_it_helps.text: The Military Lending Act rules the bill would extend cap most consumer loans for service members at a 36% annual rate including fees, and bar lenders from requiring arbitration or banning class actions, conditions that leave borrowers with no practical way to contest abuses.

analysis.who_pays: Lenders who make their money on high-cost small-dollar loans, including payday, installment, and title lenders, which could lose revenue from loans priced above 36% APR, and some borrowers might lose access to credit those lenders would stop offering.

drawbacks.text: Lenders and some economists argue a 36% cap for all borrowers would cut off small-dollar credit for people with poor credit scores, since short-term loans at that rate are less profitable to make, potentially pushing some borrowers toward unregulated lenders or bank overdraft fees.

The Military Lending Act applies to narrower loan categories than a bill extending it to 'all consumers' would; applying the cap across the entire credit market is a far larger change, and the bill has attracted only one cosponsor so far, signaling little momentum.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For most Americans, a hard 36% rate cap with arbitration limits would be a real financial protection, since rates on small-dollar loans routinely run into the hundreds of percent. The honest trade-off is that some borrowers with weak credit may find fewer lenders willing to serve them, and whether that gap gets filled by cheaper products or by worse ones is the central dispute over rate caps generally.

outcome.mechanism: It is two days old: the bill was introduced and referred to the Financial Services Committee, where it awaits a hearing or markup that has not been scheduled.

narrative.text: Representative Glenn Grothman introduced the bill on September 16, 2026, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Financial Services.
The bill has one cosponsor, a House Democrat, giving it nominal bipartisan sponsorship but very little visible support so far.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one: the bill is simply waiting in committee, and high-cost lenders are unaffected while it sits there.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; it is stalled in committee

for.name: Glenn Grothman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to extend Military Lending Act credit protections to all consumers.

sides.party_line_note: The bill has a Republican sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor, but no votes have occurred and no opposition has been recorded.

industries.note: A 36% all-in rate cap extended to all consumers would end the triple-digit-rate loans that are this industry's core product. Its interest runs against borrowers who currently pay those rates.

industries.industry: Consumer credit industry (banks, installment lenders, credit issuers)
industries.note: The bill would extend the Military Lending Act's protections, including the 36% cap and limits on arbitration clauses, to all consumers, reshaping pricing across consumer credit. Some mainstream lenders already operate below the cap; subprime-focused lenders would be hit hardest.

analysis.trajectory: With one cosponsor and only a referral to committee, the bill is unlikely to advance this session unless the Financial Services Committee takes it up; most bills introduced this late in a Congress without committee action die without a vote.
